newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti stock stabilizes after 20 percent plunge.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti stock stabilizes after 20 percent plunge.

text.p: Struggling information technology group Olivetti's stock stabilised Tuesday after Monday's plunge as markets waited for it to answer queries by stock exchange regulators about its first-half accounts.

Olivetti opened almost unchanged on the Milan bourse from its official close of 603.3 lire on Monday, when the stock suffered one of the biggest one-day falls in its history as investors wiped nearly 20 percent off the company's market value.
Brokers said the slide had been halted by investors -- who had earlier gone "short" in the company -- stepping in to snap up stock at cheaper prices in order to cover their positions.
Going short involves selling borrowed shares in anticipation that the stock will later drop, enabling the investor to buy back cheaper shares and profit on the price difference.
Analysts said they were waiting for Olivetti to deliver answers to a list of questions put to its top management on Monday evening by Consob, the stock market regulatory authority.

Consob gave Olivetti 24 hours to come up with answers to the seven questions, which it did not reveal but are known to involve details of the company's first-half results released last week. The company has not made a profit since 1990.

The current crisis of confidence in Olivetti's performance came to a head last Wednesday when the group's director general, Renzo Francesconi, resigned suddenly and made remarks casting doubt on the accuracy of the first-half figures.
That prompted Consob to suspend trading in Olivetti shares on Thursday and Friday while it called Francesconi and Olivetti's chief executive officer, Francesco Caio, to account.

Olivetti issued a statement Friday evening defending its accounting practices and saying that its figures for the first six months of 1996 were entirely in order. The company has also said it is taking legal action against Francesconi.

Investors were taken aback by a first half pre-tax loss of 440.8 billion lire ($292 million) at Olivetti, including a 200 billion ($132 million) provision to slim down money-losing parts of the business.
Foreign investors, who own around 70 percent of the group's stock, have been at the forefront of a campaign to press Olivetti to release more information about where it is going.

Olivetti is investing heavily in new businesses such as telecommunications, but cannot generate enough money from traditional ativities such as office equipment and systems integration to fund its new ventures, analysts said.
To make matters worse, its once-profitable personal computer business has guzzled cash, prompting calls from investors for it to be sold off or shut down.
